model_id: OpenAI Codex (GPT-6 family; exact serving revision unverified)

correctness_confidence.basis: The manuscript table agrees with the retained daily-peak-hour calculation. 71,326.80 and 93,104.47 divided by the common 94,059.25 reference produce 0.7583 and 0.9898. Their direct ratio is 0.7661. These conditional means survive an endpoint change.

rigor.basis: All 400 pairs have equal power and a fixed 86,400-second shift, and all 48 EIA hour endpoints have checked UTC offsets. The two-point set is explicitly conditional on the two published calendars. Neither the date of the meter nor avoided load is identified.

novelty.basis: The slide and the preprint already display the conflicting event dates. The reconstruction adds the complete value-by-value pairing and quantitative consequence for observed peak-hour load. Priority beyond the reviewed sources is uncertain.

significance.basis: The inference about temporal coincidence in a widely discussed field trial changes appreciably. The finding applies to one cluster, one grid area and two daily maxima; extrapolation to capacity accreditation would require operational evidence.

reproducibility.basis: The trial inputs and EIA export are hash-bound. Colab returned the figures and two matching builds of the reviewed PDF. The EIA URL is mutable, and the distribution includes derived EIA rows but no archival mirror of the entire historical file.

summary: I examined the three rendered pages of the exact PDF and the returned computation, checked the table against both endpoint conventions, and compared the conflicting date claims to the preprint and MassCEC slide text. The paper supports a conditional sensitivity result. I contributed to its analysis and drafting. I recommend this version as a working paper.
strengths: Power is compared across two hours of the same trace. The direct 0.7661 ratio on page 2 removes the arbitrary early-reference denominator.
Comparing the sources at fixed date separately identifies an adjacent-peak-hour effect. Both daily EIA maxima and the authors’ third-row convention are specified.
The numerical table and the qualification about avoided load are legible together on page 2. The discussion does not attribute systemwide capacity from this cluster.
weaknesses: An overlay of the 400 power observations and the two selected hour windows would make the finding easier to audit visually.
The full names and raw units of the cluster power column and a stronger provenance statement for the utility trace would aid reuse. The normalized results are insensitive to a common unit conversion.
The two published dates bracket the observed documentation conflict, but they are not a proven exhaustive set of physical dates. A dispatch identifier is still missing.
potential_errors: Interpreting 75.8% as a reduction, a fraction of full facility capacity or an avoided-load estimate would misstate the result. It is power divided by an observed early reference.
Closer agreement of EIA load with the May 3 utility series cannot validate the May 3 cluster clock. The same trace could have been replayed or relabeled.
The authors’ 1–24 hour labels lack the independent endpoint check possible for EIA. The third row is conditional on the stated convention.
strong_novelty_candidates: A timestamp discrepancy can be innocuous for a within-cluster power curve yet material for a real grid-peak join. This case supplies an empirical magnitude and a fixed-date grid-source comparison.
